mercy_translation.text:
Perhaps, being ashamed, they will agree with these things but still wish to say that if God wanted to teach and save human beings, he should have done it by a mere command and not have let his Word touch a body—just as he did at the beginning when he brought them into being from nothing.

To this objection one may reasonably answer as follows. At the beginning, when nothing yet existed anywhere, a command and mere will were sufficient for the creation of the universe. But once the human being had come into being and the need was not to create things that did not exist but to heal things already made, it was fitting for the Physician and Savior to come among those already in existence so as to heal what existed. For this reason he became a human being and used a human instrument, the body.

If it was not fitting for this to happen in this way, how was the Word, wishing to use an instrument, to come? From where was he to take it except from things already made and needing his divinity through something like themselves? It was not non-existing things that needed salvation, so that a mere command would have sufficed, but the human being already made who was being corrupted and destroyed. Therefore the Word fittingly used a human instrument and extended himself to all.

One must also know that the corruption that had taken place was not outside the body but had become attached to it. Therefore it was necessary that life should be joined to the body in place of corruption, so that just as death had come to be in the body, life also might come to be in it.

If death had been outside the body, life too would have needed to be outside it. But if death had become entangled with the body and, as though dwelling with it, held it under mastery, then life also had to be joined to the body so that, once the body had put on life, it might cast off corruption.

Otherwise, even if the Word had remained outside the body and not in it, death would naturally have been defeated by him—for death has no power against Life—but the corruption already attached to the body would nevertheless have remained in it.

For this reason the Savior fittingly clothed himself with a body, so that when the body was joined to Life it would no longer remain in death as mortal, but, having put on immortality, would rise and thereafter remain immortal. Once it had put on corruption it could not have risen unless it also put on Life. And again, death could not have been manifested by itself except in the body. Therefore he clothed himself with a body so that, finding death in the body, he might wipe it away there. For how else would the Lord have been shown to be Life unless he gave life to what was mortal?

It is like straw, which by nature is destroyed by fire. If someone merely keeps the fire away from the straw, the straw is not burned, but it still remains straw and continues to be threatened by fire, since fire naturally consumes it. But if someone clothes the straw with a great quantity of asbestos, which is said to resist fire, then the straw no longer fears the fire because it has security from its non-burning covering.

In the same way one might speak of the body and death. If death had merely been restrained by a command, the body would still have remained mortal and corruptible according to the condition of bodies. So that this would not happen, the body clothed itself with the incorporeal Word of God. Thus it no longer fears death or corruption, having Life as its garment, and corruption is made to disappear within it.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
The physician analogy distinguishes creation ex nihilo from the healing of an already existing but corrupted humanity.
The straw/asbestos image illustrates participation in the Word as the source of enduring incorruption.
